nodes.label: Magyar szólások és közmondások (O. Nagy Gábor)
nodes.author: O. Nagy Gábor
nodes.community_name: Szólások és Közmondások: Idiom & Register Tagging
nodes.norm_label: magyar szolasok es kozmondasok (o. nagy gabor)

nodes.label: Definite vs. indefinite conjugation
nodes.rationale: Used whenever the direct object is definite (definite article, ez/az, proper noun, possessive ending, 3rd-person pronoun, egymás, melyik, or unstated azt clause). This canonical grammar point recurs, retaught with different sample verbs, across nearly every source in this chunk.

nodes.label: -ik verb class
nodes.rationale: Verbs whose dictionary (3sg) form itself ends in -ik (reggelizik, zongorázik, dohányzik, hiányzik, érkezik, találkozik); stem found by stripping -ik. Prescriptively én takes -om/-em/-öm, though colloquial spoken usage often substitutes the regular indefinite ending instead — an explicit register/prescriptive-vs-actual-usage note from the source.

nodes.label: piros/vörös red color-pair political-register split
nodes.rationale: Both words mean 'red' but are not interchangeable: vörös is preferred for nature/biological referents (wine, blood, hair), institutions (Vöröskereszt), and communism/Soviet-era political referents (vörös zászló, Vörös Hadsereg, young pioneers' red scarf); piros is the register-neutral default elsewhere. Source frames this as a genuine sociolinguistic/collocational split within a single color concept that 'even fewer non-native speakers get right,' not mere synonymy. Unit 3 Cultural notes, p. 53.

nodes.label: tessék multi-use pragmatics
nodes.rationale: A single short word covering at least five distinct pragmatic functions: answering a knock, phone-answering greeting, offering food/object/seat, shop assistant's 'how can I help,' and request to repeat unclear speech, plus the doubled market-vendor call. Unit 4 Cultural notes, p. 68.

nodes.label: Coverb system (directional + perfectivizing preverbs)
nodes.rationale: Seven directional coverbs (be, fel, oda, el, ki, le, ide) attach to a verb's front to refine/redirect meaning, combine freely with motion verbs, and detach to a post-verb position whenever a focus element (negation, question word, emphasis) is introduced (the 'kicked out' rule). meg/el additionally mark perfective aspect: the Hungarian present tense can express future completion with the right coverb. tud/akar/kell/lehet/fog also displace a verb's coverb to sit before themselves. pp. 126-140, 170-171.

nodes.label: Nine-way locative case system (inside/outside/near × toward/static/from)
nodes.rationale: Hungarian has no prepositions; nine cases (a 3x3 grid) handle in/on/near, into/onto/towards, out-of/off-of/away-from. Inside cases are used for most places outside Hungary; outside cases for places within Hungary (including the country's own name) and public transport; near-by cases extend to a person's home/workplace. pp. 117-122.

nodes.label: Possessive suffix system (singular + plural possessed)
nodes.rationale: Vowel-final nouns lengthen final a/e before possessive suffixes; consonant-final nouns attach a different suffix set with unpredictable j-initial 3rd-person forms; plural-possessed uses a distinct -im/-id/-i/-ink/-itok/-ik set. Any case attaches after the possessive ending, never before. pp. 90-93, 108-109.

nodes.label: -lak/-lek 'I...you' portmanteau object conjugation
nodes.rationale: A dedicated verb ending marks the specific subject/object combination én (subject) + téged/titeket/benneteket (object), present -lak/-lek, past/subjunctive -alak/-elek; pronouns need never be stated. The chapter's own dialogue title ('Szeretlek!' 'I love you!') is built entirely around this grammar point. p. 212.

nodes.label: Past tense Class A/B/C verb-stem system
nodes.rationale: Past tense uses a short -t or long -ott/-ett/-ött marker depending on verb-stem class (A always long, B always short, C long only in 3sg indefinite), with cross-cutting exceptions in both directions and ten suppletive irregular past stems (van→volt-, jön→jött-, etc.). pp. 156-158.
nodes.norm_label: past tense class a/b/c verb-stem system

nodes.label: te/maga/ön second-person formality register system
nodes.rationale: Hungarian's three-way (six-way counting plurals) second-person formality system: te/ti (familiar), maga/maguk (neutral-to-formal default with strangers/service staff), ön/önök (most formal/official register) — maga/ön/önök take 3rd-person verb forms. The source explicitly cross-references this same system as already fully documented in the Teach Yourself Hungarian course (established/034, outside this chunk) — a same-system-confirmed-by-a-second-course finding, not a fabricated cross-chunk edge.

nodes.label: 'X, mint Y' animal/folk simile idiom cluster
nodes.rationale: A themed set of comparative similes built on mint ('like/as'): Úgy alszik, mint a mormota (sleeps like a log), Olyan ravasz, mint a róka (sly as a fox), Úgy kerüli..., mint macska a forró kását (avoids like a hot potato), Szegény, mint a templom egere (poor as a church mouse), and others — gathered by the source itself in the comparison chapter as a themed idiom set. pp. 240-241.
nodes.norm_label: 'x, mint y' animal/folk simile idiom cluster

nodes.label: Causative + potential suffix stacking
nodes.rationale: The potential ending -hat/-het combines productively with the causative -(t)at/-(t)et and ordinary personal endings in a single productive template (hív+at+hat+nál = 'you could have someone call'). Several irregular verbs (jön, megy) have no causative form at all. pp. 232-237.

nodes.label: Comparative -(a)bb/-(e)bb and superlative leg-
nodes.rationale: Comparative marked with -(a)bb/-(e)bb (several irregulars: jó→jobb, sok→több); compared item may take -nál/-nél instead of mint; degree-of-difference marked with -val/-vel on the degree noun; superlative prefixes leg- to the comparative form, not the bare adjective. pp. 238-243.

nodes.label: Conditional and past-conditional mood
nodes.rationale: Conditional ending -na/-ne; obligatory after ha, bárcsak, mintha. Past conditional formed by putting the verb in past tense and adding volna afterward. Most irregular verbs use a special conditional-only stem (van→vol-/len-, eszik→en-, iszik→in-). pp. 217-222.

nodes.label: 'Ha én rózsa volnék' — conditional mood as politically coded device
nodes.rationale: Zsuzsa Koncz's signature song (written by János Bródy) uses the conditional throughout as a politically coded device — socially/politically symbolic content veiled behind a simple flower/flag conceit — directly relevant to the chapter's own conditional-mood grammar point. Cultural notes, p. 229. A second real-world instance of Hungarian register/grammar carrying covert political meaning, alongside the piros/vörös color-register split found in established/040.
nodes.norm_label: 'ha en rozsa volnek' — conditional mood as politically coded device

nodes.label: 13-case declension system, worked across 8 noun classes
nodes.rationale: Appendix II organizes the case system as thirteen ordered case slots (nominative through terminative, plus temporal -kor handled elsewhere) worked across eight noun-stem paradigm classes (no-loss, loses-length, vowel-final, three-way vowel-harmony consonant-final, fleeting-vowel, and possessive-declension variants) — the most exhaustively tabulated case-system presentation in this project's Hungarian corpus to date. pp. 271-276.
nodes.norm_label: 13-case declension system, worked across 8 noun classes

nodes.label: Three-way static locative case system (Miben?/Min?/Minél?)
nodes.rationale: Static-location cases split into inessive (-ban/-ben, 'in what?'), superessive (-n/-on/-en/-ön, 'on what?'), and adessive (-nál/-nél, 'by/at what?'), each governed by a different verb (ül→inessive, van→superessive, áll→adessive); a parallel animate paradigm (Kiben?/Kin?/Kinél?) exists. The superessive uniquely splits three ways by vowel harmony where the other two need only two. PDF 74 (printed 73).

nodes.label: te/ön/ő pronoun register system (coarser two-way formal variant)
nodes.rationale: A three-way singular personal-pronoun system: te (informal), ön (formal, 'grammatically third person'), ő (third person, genderless). This source's two-way formal system (ön only) is coarser than the te/maga/ön three-way system documented elsewhere in this project's Hungarian corpus — no maga introduced in the sampled range. PDF 38 (printed 37).
nodes.norm_label: te/on/o pronoun register system (coarser two-way formal variant)

nodes.label: Definite/indefinite conjugation full paradigm set
nodes.rationale: Péter fut (no object, indefinite) vs. Péter lát egy autót (indefinite object, still indefinite conjugation) vs. Péter az autót látja (definite object, definite conjugation) vs. Katit várjuk (proper-noun object, definite conjugation) — the same object-definiteness-triggers-verb-agreement system anchored in established/040, retaught here with its own sample verb set. Lesson 9, pp. 215-216.

nodes.label: Past tense indicative: three conjugation classes + irregular stems
nodes.rationale: Past marker -t- splits into three classes by stem-final sound(s) (Class I linking-vowel, Class II no linking vowel, Class III linking vowel via consonant clusters/-ít/one-syllable -t verbs), plus a closed set of suppletive irregular past stems — the same class system independently documented (with different class letters) in established/042's Class A/B/C treatment of the same book series' sibling course. pp. 319-320.
nodes.norm_label: past tense indicative: three conjugation classes + irregular stems

nodes.label: Future tense: fog+infinitive (firm) vs. majd+present (open-ended)
nodes.rationale: fog + infinitive expresses intention/certainty in future action, distinguished from the more open-ended majd+present-tense construction; lesz/nem lesz supplies the suppletive future for van/nincs across locative, possessive, and predicate-nominal constructions. pp. 401-403.

nodes.label: szia/szervusz cross-source register-dating disagreement
nodes.rationale: This book's own back-matter glossary explicitly tags szia '(very familiar greeting, used mostly among young people)' but lists szervusz(tok) with no register qualifier at all — a genuine disagreement in register-marking granularity against the Teach Yourself Hungarian course (established/034, a different chunk), which explicitly frames szervusz as 'now old-fashioned' relative to szia/szevasz. Since this book (1988/1990) is the earlier publication, the disagreement suggests either that the 'datedness' judgment sharpened between 1990 and 2003, or that the two courses' authors made different editorial choices about register nuance. This mirrors the same disagreement independently observed in established/045 (also this chunk) for the same lexical item. The connection to established/034 is recorded only as a label/description note, per instruction — no cross-chunk edge is fabricated. Glossary p. 604 (PDF 605).

nodes.label: szokott + infinitive grammaticalized habitual construction
nodes.rationale: A morphologically past-tense-shaped verb form whose construction-level meaning is present-habitual; the source explicitly warns learners against the false-friend mapping to English 'used to.' p. 407.

nodes.label: Preverb system as slang-adjacent word-formation
nodes.rationale: Preverbs attach to a base verb and shift its meaning unpredictably, directly analogous to English phrasal verbs: csinál→megcsinál (fix), becsinál (vulgar 'make a mess in one's trousers'), kicsinál (slang for 'kill'), felcsinál (risqué 'get someone pregnant') — the source itself flags the vulgar/risqué double meanings deliberately. Lesson 14.

nodes.label: Communist/socialist-era institutional vocabulary cluster
nodes.rationale: Közért (genericized grocery-store name, dated to Rákosi's 1948-1956 dictatorship and 'Tessék kérni!' scarcity-era retail style), maszek (private-sector self-employed tradesman), tanács ('council,' explicitly dated 1949-1991 before polgármester 'mayor' replaced it in 1989), téesz (agricultural cooperative), and bekerül (flagged by the source as a bureaucratic-register verb 'proliferating like cancer'). A genuinely substantial, source-annotated vocabulary of Hungarian state-socialist administrative life, structurally parallel in kind to the piros/vörös political color-register split found in established/040.

nodes.label: -da/-de suffix and 19th-century language-reform (nyelvújítás) origin
nodes.rationale: Bölcsőde, óvoda, uszoda, iroda, nyomda, szálloda, cukrászda all carry a suffix the source traces to conscious 19th-century language planning — words invented by language reformers to substitute international words that would sound foreign in a non-Indo-European language. Lesson 60.

nodes.label: 23-case noun-suffix inventory (Grammatical Appendix)
nodes.rationale: Names 23 distinct case suffixes including Essive (-ul/-ül), Comitative (-stul/-stül), and two Distributive cases (-nként, -nta/-nte) not confirmed as separately captured in prior established/ Hungarian files — a fuller enumeration than the roughly 15-18 named elsewhere, and fuller in count than established/044's 13-case (+1) system from a different book in this same chunk. pp. 324-326.

nodes.label: 'Locutions' vs. 'szólások' (idioms) register taxonomy
nodes.rationale: The source distinguishes two classes of fixed multi-word expressions: locutions (invariable but semantically transparent verb+object collocations typical of formal/journalistic register, e.g. sajtótájékoztatót tart 'hold a press conference') vs. szólások (idioms proper, semantically non-compositional, e.g. csütörtököt mond). A useful register-taxonomy distinction: locutions are the formal-register analog of what slang produces informally. Lesson 81.

nodes.label: Viszontlátásra (formal) / viszlát (informal) goodbye register pair
nodes.rationale: The clearest explicit register-tagged minimal pair found in the sampled back-matter glossary, directly parallel to the szia/szervusz and krumpli/burgonya pairs documented from Teach Yourself Hungarian (established/034, out of this chunk). Hungarian-English glossary p. 296; English-Hungarian glossary p. 299.

nodes.label: szervusz glossed as plain informal greeting with no generational/period marking
nodes.rationale: This 1990 source glosses szervusz as a plain informal greeting/farewell with no generational marking, unlike the Teach Yourself Hungarian course's (established/034, out of this chunk) explicit 2003 note that szervusz is now old-fashioned relative to szia/szevasz. Since this source predates TYH by 13 years, this is plausibly a genuine period snapshot: the 'dated' register marking on szervusz may itself be a development of the 1990s-2000s rather than already true in 1990. Not a fabricated cross-chunk edge — the connection to established/034 is recorded only in this label/description, per instruction.

nodes.label: Derivational Order Meaningful, Inflectional Order Fixed
nodes.rationale: Kornai's sharp generalization (§4.1.2): reordering inflectional suffix classes (tense/mood vs. person/number/definiteness) generates identical meaning regardless of order - a historical-convention fact, not a grammatical necessity. Reordering derivational suffixes (frequentative vs. causative/factitive) changes meaning/scope (sajtó cserélgetteti vs. cseréltetgeti). This is the theoretical generalization that Rounds' olvastathat/olvasgathat causative+potential/frequentative+potential examples instantiate directly, and is flagged in the extraction checklist as a plausible mechanism for future morphological_play slang analysis.
nodes.norm_label: derivational order meaningful, inflectional order fixed

nodes.label: Lowering Diacritic / Lowering Stems (Kornai)
nodes.rationale: Kornai's central empirical finding: many productive suffixes (1st/2nd sg. possessive, past/imperative/conditional markers, -as/-es/-os/-ös) silently carry a 'lowering' (ML) diacritic that only becomes visible once a further suffix stacks on top, turning an ordinary Class II/V stem into a 'lowering stem' for whatever attaches next. Lexicalization can strip this marking (házas vs. freshly-derived házasakat). Flagship morphological finding for this language, per explicit dispatch instruction.

nodes.label: Potential/Causative/Frequentative Endings
nodes.rationale: Three productive verbal derivational endings (-hat/-het potential, -at/-et~-tat/-tet causative, -gat/-get frequentative) each redefine the verb stem, after which further derivational/inflectional morphology (including each other) attaches to the NEW stem, not the original. All three combine with the potential (olvastathat, olvasgathat), and causative+frequentative reordering (cserélgetteti vs. cseréltetgeti) changes scope of repetition, unlike inflectional-suffix reordering which is meaning-neutral. Flagship morphological finding for this language, per explicit dispatch instruction.

nodes.label: Coverb+verb idiomatic-opacity pattern (kicsinál/átver)
nodes.rationale: kicsinál ('kill, finish off,' lit. 'do-out') and átver ('cheat on someone,' lit. 'beat-across') are the source's own examples of semantically opaque coverb+verb combinations, both landing in colloquial/informal registers — a coverb-driven idiom-formation pattern distinct from clipping or straightforward morphological derivation. p. 57.
nodes.community_name: Hungarian Verbs & Practical Grammar: Verb Morphology

nodes.label: Reflexive verb-forming suffixes as their own productive category
nodes.rationale: Four suffix-shape families (-kodik/-kedik/-ködik, -kozik/-kezik/-közik, -ódik/-ődik, -ó(d)zik/-ő(d)zik) form a dedicated productive derivational category, with an explicit note that not every verb bearing one of these shapes is semantically reflexive (jelentkezik 'report/apply,' gondolkozik 'think'). Ch. 12.
nodes.community_name: Hungarian Verbs & Practical Grammar: Verb Morphology
nodes.norm_label: reflexive verb-forming suffixes as their own productive category

nodes.label: Verb Index as reverse-lookup morphological classification key
nodes.rationale: The book's closing nine pages let a learner take an encountered verb and find which paradigm-table it patterns after, organized tense-by-tense and mood-by-mood by phonological stem class — a systematic verb-to-class cross-reference tool that neither Rounds, FSI, nor TYH provide in this direction (they only go class-to-example). pp. 129-137.
nodes.community_name: Hungarian Verbs & Practical Grammar: Verb Morphology
nodes.norm_label: verb index as reverse-lookup morphological classification key

nodes.label: Complex verb construction (nominal + van, missing copula)
nodes.rationale: kénytelen+VAN, képes+VAN, köteles+VAN, kész+VAN, hajlandó+VAN — nominal + conjugated van, missing the copula in the present 3rd person (Ő kész meghalni but Ők készek meghalni). Named alongside a closed list of 'separator' verbs (akar, bír, fog, kell, lehet, mer, óhajt, szabad+VAN, szeretne, szokott, tetszik, tud) that control preverb-placement in infinitival constructions. Ch. 23.5.
nodes.community_name: Hungarian Verbs & Practical Grammar: Verb Morphology
nodes.norm_label: complex verb construction (nominal + van, missing copula)

nodes.label: Systematic postposition orientation/meaning/usage table
nodes.rationale: A dedicated Postpositions chapter (Ch. 5) gives a full orientation/meaning/usage table (előtt/elé/elől, mögött/mögé/mögül, alatt/alá/alól, etc.) crossed with SPACE/TIME/ABSTRACT domains, plus the postpositional-pronominal paradigm — presented as its own systematic unit distinct from the case system.

nodes.rationale: The full 2sg conjunctive-imperative of 'come' is explicitly called practically extinct in colloquial Hungarian, with gyertek (2pl) marked 'more colloquial than the long form jöjjetek' — the grammar reference itself, not a conversational-course culture note, making the colloquial-register call explicitly. p. 42.

nodes.label: focizik — denominal -ik verb from clipped sport-name noun
nodes.rationale: 'To play football' — a denominal -ik verb built from foci, itself a recognizable colloquial clipping of futball/labdarúgás, paralleling clipping-based slang formation documented elsewhere in the corpus. A second, denominal-verb-formation route into informal vocabulary, distinct from the coverb-idiom route (kicsinál/átver) flagged in established/051.
